chapters.title: The Platform and the Bet: Septerna's Strategic Position at the GPCR Frontier
chapters.body:
On the first day of July 2025, Novo Nordisk A/S transferred $195 million to Septerna Inc.'s account — the upfront payment activating a four-program research collaboration that the two companies had announced six weeks earlier. The wire was not a licensing fee for proven drugs or a royalty on marketed products. It was payment for access to a platform: a proprietary bioengineering system that reconstitutes G protein-coupled receptors outside the cell while preserving the molecular partners and membrane environment they require to behave as they do in living tissue. That Novo Nordisk, the company that remade the global obesity landscape with GLP-1 receptor agonists, chose to pay one of the largest discovery-stage upfront fees in recent biotech history to study GLP-1R through someone else's lens said something unambiguous about what that platform was worth.

## Three Propositions, One Bet

The investment thesis underpinning this dossier rests on three interlocking claims. First, the GPCR target class remains the most validated yet systematically underleveraged frontier in small-molecule drug discovery: approximately one-third of all FDA-approved drugs act on GPCRs, yet roughly 300 clinically relevant members of the superfamily remain pharmacologically inaccessible because conventional biochemistry cannot capture them in their native, pharmacologically productive conformations. Second, Septerna's Native Complex Platform constitutes a genuine structural and functional breakthrough — not an incremental improvement on existing tools, but an approach that reconstitutes full receptor complexes at industrial scale, opening those 300 targets to cryo-electron microscopy, fragment-based screening, and allosteric site mapping in ways that were not previously achievable. Third, the company has assembled the capital resources, scientific credibility, and commercial partnerships to execute simultaneous clinical validation across multiple programs — transforming from a discovery vehicle into a multi-asset clinical-stage enterprise before the decade closes.

The Novo Nordisk deal tests the first two propositions simultaneously. The $195 million upfront, against a total potential deal value of approximately $2.2 billion ~~across four programs targeting GLP-1R, GIPR, the glucagon receptor, and a fourth undisclosed cardiometabolic GPCR~~ ==across four simultaneous research programs spanning five cardiometabolic GPCR collaboration targets, including GLP-1R, GIPR, and the glucagon receptor==, implies that the world's dominant GLP-1 innovator concluded that Septerna's platform could access structural and allosteric space on receptors Novo had been studying for decades — space that Novo's own discovery infrastructure could not reliably reach.

## The Intellectual Foundation

Septerna was incorporated in December 2019 under the name GPCR NewCo, Inc., incubated from inception by Third Rock Ventures in Boston. The renamed entity launched publicly in January 2022 with a $100 million Series A and a founding scientific cohort assembled around Chief Executive Officer Jeffrey Finer, MD, PhD — a physician-scientist and former Third Rock entrepreneur-in-residence who had been the primary architect of the Native Complex Platform concept. The scientific advisory board at formation included Robert Lefkowitz, the Duke University biochemist whose decades of GPCR structural and signaling research earned him the 2012 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, alongside Arthur Christopoulos and Patrick Sexton, two of the foremost GPCR pharmacologists working today. That lineage — Nobel Prize-rooted science, translated by a management team with drug-development operational fluency — established the credibility that made the Novo Nordisk partnership legible to a large pharmaceutical counterparty.

## The Snapshot

As of the frozen date of May 23, 2026, Septerna presented the following profile:

|---|---|
| Cash & marketable securities (Q1 2026) | $522.1 million |
| Market capitalization | ~$1.25 billion |
| Cash runway (management guidance) | At least through 2029 |
| Q1 2026 collaboration revenue (annualized run-rate) | ~$106 million |
| Novo Nordisk collaboration — upfront received | $195 million |
| Novo Nordisk collaboration — total potential value | ~$2.2 billion |
| Lead immunology asset | SEP-631 (MRGPRX2 NAM, Phase 2b-ready in CSU) |
| Lead endocrinology asset | SEP-479 (PTH1R agonist, Phase 1 active) |
| Preclinical program | TSHR NAM for Graves' disease |

[Septerna Q1 2026 earnings release](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2026/05/11/3292284/0/en/Septerna-Highlights-Business-Progress-and-Reports-First-Quarter-2026-Financial-Results.html)

The balance sheet carries no debt. The $195 million Novo upfront arrived on top of the $302.6 million in net IPO proceeds raised in October 2024, producing a capital position with no near-term dilution requirement under the base clinical execution plan. The collaboration's FTE-based research services billings added a further $18.6 million to FY2025 revenue against the $26.8 million recognized from upfront amortization — a revenue profile that will expand in FY2026 as the first full fiscal year of the collaboration is captured.

## What Comes Next

Each of these numbers is a premise rather than a conclusion. The Phase 2b trial of SEP-631 in chronic spontaneous urticaria, planned to initiate in the second half of 2026, will deliver the first external, patient-level efficacy readout of a compound discovered entirely through the Native Complex Platform — the moment at which the platform's clinical productivity graduates from hypothesis to evidence.

chapters.title: Incubation, Launch, and Acceleration: Septerna's Journey from GPCR NewCo to NASDAQ
chapters.body:
## Origins in the GPCR Laboratory

The company that would eventually trade on Nasdaq under the ticker SEPN began not as a startup pitch but as a question posed inside Third Rock Ventures' South San Francisco offices in late 2019: if Nobel laureate Robert Lefkowitz's decades of structural work on G protein-coupled receptors represented the most important advance in receptor pharmacology of the twentieth century, why had it yielded so few new medicines?

Lefkowitz, whose 2012 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded jointly with Brian Kobilka for elucidating how GPCRs sense their environment and transmit signals into cells, had established the mechanistic foundations. GPCRs—a superfamily of roughly 800 receptors sharing a characteristic architecture of seven alpha-helical segments threading the cell membrane—regulate virtually every physiological process the human body performs, from the rhythm of a heartbeat to the secretion of insulin to the pruning of an immune response. Approximately one-third of all FDA-approved drugs act on members of this family. Yet that success rate applied to perhaps two hundred of the most structurally tractable targets. Another three hundred or so GPCRs with known therapeutic relevance remained inaccessible, not because the biology was uninteresting but because conventional biochemistry stripped these receptors of the molecular partners—associated G proteins, beta-arrestins, membrane lipids—that they require to adopt the precise conformational states a drug must engage.

Jeffrey Finer, then a partner and entrepreneur-in-residence at Third Rock, believed the solution was industrial rather than academic. The question was whether a platform could be built to reconstitute full receptor complexes outside the cell at sufficient scale and fidelity to support modern drug discovery tools: cryo-electron microscopy for structural elucidation, fragment-based screening, allosteric binding-site mapping. In December 2019, Third Rock incorporated the answer as GPCR NewCo, Inc.

## A Name Carrying Scientific Intent

For the better part of a year and a half, the entity existed as a named shell around a growing research team and an emerging proprietary methodology. In June 2021, as the infrastructure matured, the company renamed itself Septerna, Inc. The etymology was deliberate: *septem*, the Latin root for seven, embedded directly into the corporate identity as a permanent reference to the seven-transmembrane helix architecture that defines every GPCR and every target the company would ever pursue. Naming conventions in biotech tend to be either arbitrary or aggressively aspirational; Septerna's was unusual in being structurally descriptive—a signal to sophisticated investors that the founders understood the science precisely enough to put it in the corporate letterhead.

## The Series A and the Public Launch

On January 27, 2022, Septerna formally emerged from stealth with the announcement of a $100 million Series A financing round led by Third Rock Ventures. The round's size was notable for a platform-stage company without clinical assets, and the scientific pitch materials reflected this: the launch was organized not around a lead drug candidate but around the Native Complex Platform itself—the proprietary bioengineering system that Finer and his colleagues argued constituted a structural and functional breakthrough in GPCR biochemistry.

Third Rock's co-investors in the Series A were not disclosed in granular detail at launch, but the scientific advisory cohort anchoring the announcement carried its own persuasive weight. Robert Lefkowitz joined as an advisor alongside Arthur Christopoulos, PhD, and Patrick Sexton, PhD, DSc, two of the most cited GPCR pharmacologists in the world. The combination of Lefkowitz's Nobel imprimatur with Christopoulos and Sexton's active laboratory expertise was intended to signal that the platform had been stress-tested against the highest available scientific standard.

Finer, newly appointed Chief Executive Officer, framed the Native Complex Platform at launch as a qualitative shift in what was chemically tractable. The argument was simple in structure if complex in execution: access to structurally native receptor complexes meant access to binding pockets that simply did not form—and therefore could not be screened against—when receptors were studied in isolation. The implication was that Septerna had first-mover access to chemistry space that remained invisible to every competitor working with conventional purified receptor preparations.

## The Series B and Pipeline Validation

By the summer of 2023, Septerna had advanced its internal pipeline sufficiently to justify a larger financing. In July of that year, the company closed a $150 million Series B led by RA Capital Management, the Boston-based investment firm with one of the more intensive analytical franchises in institutional biotech. New investors included Deep Track Capital and BVF Partners, both specialist biotech funds whose participation signals independent diligence rather than follow-on loyalty. Existing investors including Third Rock maintained their positions.

The Series B was fifty percent larger than the Series A, a step-up that reflected both the valuation progression and, critically, early scientific data on two programs: SEP-786, the first-generation PTH1R agonist for hypoparathyroidism, and SEP-631, a negative allosteric modulator of MRGPRX2 for inflammatory mast cell disorders. Neither compound had yet entered human subjects, but the preclinical pharmacology—particularly the structural data enabled by the Native Complex Platform—was compelling enough for RA Capital to lead rather than follow. The message implicit in the Series B's structure was that platform credibility could precede clinical proof-of-concept if the underlying science was rigorous enough.

## IPO on Nasdaq

Septerna filed for its initial public offering in October 2024, choosing a market environment that had grown selectively receptive to platform-stage biotechs with differentiated mechanisms and near-term catalysts. The company priced 18.4 million shares, including the full exercise of the overallotment option, at $18.00 per share on October 25, 2024, generating gross proceeds of $331.2 million and net proceeds of approximately $302.6 million after underwriting discounts.

The bookrunner roster—J.P. Morgan, TD Cowen, Cantor Fitzgerald, and Wells Fargo Securities—represented a credible distribution network across the institutional biotech buyer base. The upsizing of the offering from its initial range marked the transaction as one of the largest biotech IPOs of the fourth quarter of 2024, a period in which the sector was navigating renewed interest rate uncertainty and selective investor appetite. The proceeds gave Septerna a cash position that, combined with Series B reserves and subsequent collaboration revenue, would extend operating runway through at least 2029—a critical buffer for a company managing simultaneous Phase 1 programs and preparing for Phase 2b.

## The SEP-786 Discontinuation: Platform Under Pressure

The first serious test of Septerna's scientific narrative arrived three months after the IPO. In February 2025, the company announced the discontinuation of SEP-786 following observations in two patients during the Phase 1 multiple ascending dose cohort: both experienced reversible Grade 3 unconjugated bilirubin elevations, a laboratory finding that indicated hepatic stress. Subsequent mechanistic characterization identified SEP-786 as a potent inhibitor of UGT1A1, a liver enzyme involved in bilirubin conjugation. The liability was structural rather than target-related—SEP-786's PTH1R agonist activity was never in question—but the compound carried an off-target interaction that made clinical development untenable.

The discontinuation was a meaningful early setback for a company whose IPO story had centered on the platform's ability to generate superior molecules precisely because structural access to native receptor complexes should reduce off-target liabilities. The question in investor communications was whether the UGT1A1 finding reflected a systematic gap in the Native Complex Platform's screening approach or a one-time chemical accident in the first-generation compound.

Management's response—pivoting immediately to SEP-479, a next-generation PTH1R agonist designed from the outset to eliminate UGT1A1 inhibitory activity—was a calculated demonstration that the platform could generate backup candidates on a timeline shorter than the industry average. SEP-479 had been discovered using the same Native Complex methodology and was characterized in part through the same structural biology infrastructure. Its existence and readiness for Phase 1 initiation (which followed in April 2026) became the primary counter-narrative to the SEP-786 setback.

## The Novo Nordisk Alliance as Capstone

Whatever residual skepticism the SEP-786 discontinuation left in the institutional investor community was substantially addressed on May 14, 2025, when Septerna announced a research collaboration with Novo Nordisk A/S covering ~~four simultaneous cardiometabolic GPCR programs: GLP-1R, GIPR, the glucagon receptor, and an undisclosed fourth target,~~ ==four simultaneous cardiometabolic GPCR R&D programs spanning five collaboration targets,== all in obesity and related metabolic conditions. Novo Nordisk paid $195 million upfront on July 1, 2025, assumed all downstream R&D costs at the IND-enabling stage, and committed to milestones that bring total potential value to approximately $2.2 billion.

The strategic logic of the deal was unmistakable. Novo Nordisk was not option-buying; it was purchasing proprietary discovery access to the structural and allosteric chemical space on receptors that defined its own most commercially critical therapeutic area. That the world's dominant GLP-1 innovator concluded that Septerna's platform could map binding sites ~~on GLP-1R and GIPR~~ ==across this cluster of incretin and metabolic GPCRs== that its internal capabilities could not constituted a form of third-party validation that no investor presentation could replicate.

In the five and a half years from its incorporation as a two-word placeholder inside a venture firm to a Nasdaq-listed company anchored by a landmark partnership, Septerna had converted one Nobel laureate's structural biology into a funded clinical pipeline, a $331 million public offering, and a $2.2 billion collaboration with the most commercially powerful company in modern endocrinology.

chapters.title: The Native Complex Platform and the Pipeline It Built: GPCRs from Structure to Clinic
chapters.body:
## Reconstituting the Receptor: What the Native Complex Platform Actually Does

The scientific problem Septerna was built to solve is older than the company by decades. G protein-coupled receptors are the largest superfamily of membrane proteins in the human genome—more than 800 members, responsible for mediating virtually every class of extracellular signal, from hormones and neurotransmitters to odorants and photons. Approximately one-third of all FDA-approved small-molecule drugs act on GPCRs, a commercial record unmatched by any other target class. Yet despite this validation, roughly 300 clinically relevant GPCRs have resisted systematic small-molecule discovery, not because they are unimportant but because they are structurally inaccessible by the methods the industry has historically relied upon.

The difficulty is architectural. GPCRs are inherently unstable outside the plasma membrane. They require their signal-transducing partners—heterotrimeric G proteins on the intracellular face, beta-arrestins for signal termination, and the specific phospholipid composition of the native bilayer—to adopt the conformational states that matter pharmacologically. Remove those partners, and the receptor collapses into a poorly folded, functionally ambiguous preparation that may bind a radiolabeled ligand in an assay but bears little resemblance to the protein a drug will encounter in a patient's cell.

Conventional GPCR biochemistry addressed this problem by simplification: truncate the receptor to its most stable domain, solubilize it in detergent to strip the membrane, fuse it to a thermostabilizing scaffold, and co-crystallize it with a nanobody to lock a single conformation. This approach produced the structural insights that won Robert Lefkowitz and Brian Kobilka the 2012 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, and it has generated validated drugs. But it is also the reason so many GPCRs remain undrugged—detergent-solubilized, truncated preparations are simply not accessible to the full pharmacological toolkit. Fragment-based screening, which requires large quantities of correctly folded, functional protein; high-throughput screening against allosteric sites, which only form in the presence of intracellular partners; and cryo-electron microscopy structural determination of the receptor in multiple signaling conformations—all of these demand what conventional methods cannot provide: a GPCR that behaves as if it were still in the cell.

The Native Complex Platform produces exactly that. The technology reconstitutes full-length GPCRs in lipid nanoparticles—synthetic membrane discs whose lipid composition is tuned to mimic the plasma membrane bilayer—together with their relevant G protein subtypes and beta-arrestins. The result is a stable, functional receptor assembly that can be produced in quantities sufficient for industrial-scale operations: milligram quantities of correctly folded complex, amenable to cryo-EM structural determination at high resolution, compatible with fragment libraries numbering in the tens of thousands, and scalable to high-throughput screening formats. The platform effectively transforms previously intractable receptors into tractable ones, unlocking the same discovery toolkit that has been applied to kinases, proteases, and ion channels for decades.

The cryo-EM capability is particularly consequential. Because the Native Complex preserves multiple receptor conformations—the active state stabilized by a G protein, the intermediate state associated with arrestin recruitment, the basal state in the absence of agonist—structural biologists can map the full conformational landscape of a target receptor. This is where allosteric sites become visible. Orthosteric sites, the binding pockets where endogenous ligands dock, are by definition occupied by evolution-optimized molecules; designing selective small molecules to compete with them is difficult, and the risk of cross-reactivity with related receptors sharing the same orthosteric chemistry is substantial. Allosteric sites, which are topographically distinct from the orthosteric pocket and vary in three-dimensional architecture across even closely related receptor subtypes, offer superior selectivity handles. They can amplify, dampen, or modulate the character of an agonist signal without displacing the endogenous ligand—a pharmacological sophistication particularly valuable in endocrinology and immunology, where partial agonism or biased signaling may be therapeutically preferable to full activation or complete blockade. The Native Complex Platform, by resolving receptor structure in multiple states, makes these sites mappable and, critically, druggable.

## SEP-631: MRGPRX2 and the Proof-of-Mechanism in Mast Cells

The first asset to reach clinical validation was SEP-631, a negative allosteric modulator of MRGPRX2, a GPCR expressed on mast cells that mediates IgE-independent degranulation. MRGPRX2 sits at the intersection of urticaria biology and the emerging understanding that a substantial fraction of chronic spontaneous urticaria cases involve IgE-independent mast cell activation that ~~omalizumab and other anti-IgE therapies~~ ==omalizumab and the IL-4Rα biologic dupilumab (Dupixent, FDA-approved for CSU on April 18, 2025)== do not adequately address. Blocking MRGPRX2 with an oral small molecule would theoretically suppress this mechanism without the immunological breadth of biologics ==— a mechanism Evommune's EVO756, characterized by primary sources as an MRGPRX2 antagonist, is already advancing in Phase 2b for CSU, and a category in which Rhapsido has already secured FDA approval as an oral CSU treatment==.

The Phase 1 data, reported in 2025, provided the most concrete early demonstration of what the Native Complex Platform can discover. SEP-631 administered once daily produced dose-dependent, near-complete suppression of icatibant-induced skin wheal responses across a 10–200 mg dose range, with complete inhibition observed at the 10 mg dose. Icatibant, a bradykinin B2 receptor ~~agonist~~ ==antagonist==, triggers MRGPRX2-mediated mast cell degranulation when injected intradermally; the wheal it produces is a validated pharmacodynamic readout of MRGPRX2 activity. Clean suppression across the dose range confirmed both target engagement and oral bioavailability, validating the core discovery output of the platform. A Phase 2b trial in chronic spontaneous urticaria is planned for the second half of 2026, making SEP-631 the company's nearest-term efficacy readout in patients.

## SEP-479 and the PTH1R Program: Backup Candidate as Platform Validation

Septerna's second clinical asset emerged from a setback that, counterintuitively, strengthened the case for the platform rather than undermining it. SEP-786, a first-generation oral PTH1R agonist for hypoparathyroidism, entered Phase 1 in 2024 and was discontinued in February 2025 after two patients in a multiple ascending dose cohort developed Grade 3 unconjugated bilirubin elevations attributable to potent UGT1A1 inhibition—an off-target hepatic enzyme effect unrelated to PTH1R biology. The company's characterization of the mechanism was straightforward: SEP-786's chemical scaffold carried a UGT1A1 liability independent of its receptor activity, a solvable medicinal chemistry problem rather than a biological dead end.

SEP-479, disclosed as a structurally distinct PTH1R agonist designed de novo on the Native Complex Platform to eliminate UGT1A1 inhibitory activity, entered Phase 1 dosing in April 2026. The speed of the backup generation—from SEP-786 discontinuation in February 2025 to clinical dosing of a successor approximately fourteen months later—illustrates one of the platform's industrial claims: because the full receptor complex with its co-bound G proteins and arrestins is available at scale, lead optimization cycles can be run against functional conformations rather than surrogate assays, compressing the medicinal chemistry iteration required to address a specific liability.

Hypoparathyroidism remains an indication with genuine unmet need. Current standard of care is calcium and vitamin D supplementation combined, in some patients, with ~~the injectable PTH peptide analogue teriparatide or the recombinant human PTH 1-84~~ ==palopegteriparatide (Yorvipath), a once-daily subcutaneous PTH replacement that supplanted recombinant human PTH 1-84 (NATPARA) after Takeda announced manufacturing discontinuation at the end of 2024==. No approved oral therapy exists. An oral PTH1R agonist that replaces peptide-level hormonal activity would represent a meaningful clinical advance, and the PTH1R binding mode discovered through the Native Complex Platform—positive allosteric modulation that activates the receptor through a site distinct from the orthosteric peptide-binding cavity—is designed to provide stable, sustained agonism with a small-molecule pharmacokinetic profile.

## TSHR NAM and the Preclinical Frontier

The third internal asset, a thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor negative allosteric modulator being developed for Graves' disease, remains in preclinical development candidate selection as of the frozen snapshot date. Graves' disease is an autoimmune hyperthyroidism driven by antibody-mediated TSHR activation; current treatment options—antithyroid drugs, radioiodine ablation, and thyroidectomy—address the downstream consequence of excessive thyroid hormone rather than the autoimmune TSHR activation itself. A selective TSHR NAM that blocks antibody-driven receptor activity while permitting regulated TSH signaling would address the pathophysiological mechanism directly. The Native Complex Platform's ability to resolve TSHR in its antibody-bound and antibody-free conformations provides a structural basis for designing allosteric modulators that discriminate between TSH-driven and autoantibody-driven signaling states—a selectivity problem that conventional TSHR biochemistry has not been able to adequately address.

## The Novo Nordisk Collaboration: Why the World's GLP-1 Leader Concluded It Needed Septerna

The Novo Nordisk collaboration, signed May 14, 2025, and effective July 1, 2025, covers four simultaneous ~~programs targeting GLP-1R, GIPR, the glucagon receptor, and a fourth undisclosed cardiometabolic GPCR~~ ==R&D programs spanning five collaboration targets, anchored on GLP-1R, GIPR, and the glucagon receptor alongside additional undisclosed cardiometabolic GPCRs==. The $195 million upfront payment—one of the largest discovery-stage collaboration fees in recent biotech history—reflects a specific strategic conclusion by Novo Nordisk's leadership: that oral small-molecule agonists for GLP-1R, GIPR, and the glucagon receptor are strategically essential in a market where injectable peptides dominate, and that the Native Complex Platform could access receptor conformations and allosteric sites that internal Novo capabilities could not.

The technical rationale is specific. GLP-1R, GIPR, and the glucagon receptor are class B1 GPCRs—a subfamily defined by large extracellular domains and a signaling architecture that is difficult to reconstitute with conventional detergent biochemistry. Their pharmacologically productive conformations require interactions with Gs proteins and the membrane environment to be maintained. The allosteric space on these receptors—binding pockets that can potentiate or modulate agonist-driven signaling at residues distant from the orthosteric peptide-binding groove—is structurally accessible only when the full native complex is assembled. Structure Therapeutics, which has advanced an oral small-molecule GLP-1R modulator through early development using a different reconstitution approach, represents a proof of concept that the allosteric space on class B GPCRs exists and is druggable; Septerna's platform claim is that it can access this space more broadly, across multiple receptor subtypes simultaneously, with the throughput to generate development candidates on a timescale relevant to partnership milestones.

The collaboration's four-program structure is an explicit test of that claim. Novo Nordisk did not license a single asset; it contracted Septerna to apply the platform systematically across ~~four~~ ==five== of the most commercially important GPCR targets in human medicine. The $2.2 billion in total potential milestones reflects not a single binary readout but a sustained multi-year discovery and development partnership whose economics scale with the platform's demonstrated productivity. Septerna retains a co-profit-share option on one program and tiered royalties across all four—a financial architecture designed to align the partnership's long-term incentives with the company's platform validation goals.

---

Taken together, the Native Complex Platform's three commercial expressions—an internally advanced clinical pipeline, a backup candidate generation capability validated by SEP-479's rapid emergence after SEP-786's discontinuation, and a discovery collaboration with the world's leading GPCR drug developer—constitute the operational case for Septerna's platform thesis. Each program run against a previously intractable receptor, each allosteric site mapped, and each development candidate generated adds to a compounding body of evidence that the 300 undrugged GPCRs are not an insoluble problem but a structural one—and that the Native Complex Platform has, at minimum, begun to solve it.

chapters.title: The Economics of a Discovery Engine: Revenue Recognition, Cash Burn, and Capital Structure
chapters.body:
## A Revenue Line That Did Not Exist Two Years Ago

For most of its early life, Septerna Inc. generated essentially no revenue. In fiscal year 2024, the South San Francisco-based GPCR drug discovery company reported $1.1 million in collaboration income—a token figure from early research services agreements, dwarfed by an operating loss of $71.8 million. Twelve months later, that picture had been transformed by a single commercial transaction. For fiscal year 2025, Septerna recorded [$46.0 million in total revenue](https://ir.septerna.com/news-releases/news-release-details/septerna-highlights-pipeline-progress-and-reports-fourth-quarter-and)—a 41-fold increase—driven almost entirely by the Novo Nordisk collaboration that closed on July 1, 2025.

The accounting mechanics matter. When Novo Nordisk paid the $195 million upfront fee, Septerna did not recognise all of it immediately. Under ASC 606, the revenue recognition standard for contracts with customers, the company was required to identify its distinct performance obligations under the agreement—the research activities, licenses, and program delivery commitments embedded across ~~four cardiometabolic targets~~ ==four simultaneous R&D programs spanning five cardiometabolic collaboration targets==—and allocate the transaction price accordingly. The upfront payment was recorded as a deferred revenue liability on the balance sheet and is being amortised into the income statement over the estimated performance period. Separately, the delivery of full-time-equivalent research services to Novo Nordisk—the scientists, screens, and structural biology work billed on a cost-plus or contractual FTE basis—is recognised on a more contemporaneous, effort-based schedule.

The result for the six months from collaboration effective date to year-end 2025: $26.8 million in upfront amortisation plus $18.6 million in research services billings, totalling the $46.0 million reported for the full fiscal year. The revenue is entirely collaboration-derived; Septerna has no approved products, no royalty streams, and no product sales. The single-customer concentration is stark, intentional, and well-understood by investors who followed the IPO roadshow.

## The 2025 Income Statement in Detail

A line-by-line walk through the fiscal year 2025 results reveals a company investing aggressively in clinical execution even as the collaboration provides meaningful offset.
